title: IBS and finding a toilet when you are away from home
description: Practical toilet planning for people with IBS: check nearby bathrooms, opening hours and access before going out, and know when to seek medical advice.
author: Chcę Siku! editorial team
lead: If you have irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), knowing where to find a toilet can make a walk, meeting or journey easier to organise. Check a suitable toilet near your destination, how to get inside and one alternative nearby. This is practical preparation to use alongside appropriate care; it does not treat IBS.

sections.heading: Why can toilet access matter with IBS?
sections.html:
IBS can involve recurring abdominal pain and changes in bowel movements, including diarrhoea, constipation or both. Some people also experience bloating or a feeling that they have not fully emptied their bowel. With diarrhoea, the need for a toilet can be sudden. Symptoms vary between people and from one day to another. The NIDDK guide to IBS symptoms explains these differences.

Frequent toilet visits do not automatically mean IBS. A healthcare professional needs to assess the cause. Even after a diagnosis, new or substantially different symptoms should not simply be assumed to be the same condition. Finding a nearby bathroom and understanding a health problem are separate tasks.

sections.heading: Plan around your destination, not just your starting point
sections.html:
Look for a toilet near the station where you will arrive, the museum you are visiting or the place where you are meeting friends. For a longer journey, check a possible stop along the way too. Find out when the toilet opens and whether entry requires a ticket, purchase or payment. A pin on a map cannot answer every question about access.

Choose one main option and one backup. Save the address or a screenshot of useful details if you expect a poor internet connection. A saved address helps you find the building; it does not confirm that the toilet will be open when you arrive. If reliable access is especially important, contact the venue beforehand.

When arranging a meeting, it is enough to say, “I need somewhere with easy access to a toilet.” You do not have to explain your medical history to everyone to choose a suitable place.

sections.heading: The nearest toilet may not be the easiest to reach
sections.html:
A toilet 150 metres away might be behind a ticket barrier, upstairs or deep inside a shopping centre. A slightly more distant option with a direct street entrance may be more practical. Compare distance with the entrance, opening hours and conditions of use. Check step-free access separately if you need it.

Consider the route as well. A busy road, railway line or closed passage can make the walk longer than the straight-line distance suggests. Use the map to orient yourself, then follow signs and actual access routes. A member of staff may be able to clarify an entrance more quickly than another search.

sections.heading: Prepare for the day without changing treatment on your own
sections.html:
There is no single diet or medicine that suits everyone with IBS. A brief record of meals and symptoms can help a discussion with a professional. If symptoms persist or you need to exclude many foods, speak to a doctor or dietitian. The NHS guide to diet, lifestyle and medicines for IBS explains when further advice may help.

Pack the things you normally need: a charged phone, hygiene supplies, water and any prescribed medicines. Follow your existing treatment instructions rather than changing doses for a trip. Allow time to walk and take a break, without needing to schedule every minute of the day.

sections.heading: When should you seek medical advice?
sections.html:
Arrange a consultation if recurring bowel symptoms have not been assessed, your usual treatment is no longer helping, or symptoms are preventing work, social plans or travel. It can help to note when the problem started, changes in your bowel habits and medicines you take.

Rectal bleeding or bloody diarrhoea, unexplained significant weight loss, or a hard lump or swelling in your abdomen need urgent medical assessment. Do not assume these are an ordinary IBS flare-up. These are among the warning signs in the NHS overview of IBS symptoms. Use urgent medical services if you become suddenly or seriously unwell.

sections.heading: How can Chcę Siku! help with toilet planning?
sections.html:
Chcę Siku! helps you find nearby toilets, read available details and see the direction to a chosen place. Check whether the facilities match your needs before setting off. Opening hours and access can change, so a listing cannot guarantee that a toilet is available at all times.

After a visit, a factual review can help the next person: describe the entrance, cleanliness or access rules without sharing private health information. Download Chcę Siku! or read our step-by-step app guide. For planning a journey, see how to find toilets while travelling.

This article provides general information and practical planning suggestions. It is not a diagnosis or individual medical advice.

NHS - Diet, lifestyle and medicines for IBS

title: Anxiety about finding a toilet in an unfamiliar place
description: Worried you will not find a toilet when you go out? A practical plan for unfamiliar places, the limits of toilet maps and when to seek professional help.
author: Chcę Siku! editorial team
lead: “What if I need a toilet and cannot find one?” This worry can come up before a journey, meeting or walk somewhere unfamiliar. Checking toilet access can help with the practical arrangements. If fear increasingly limits your life, professional support can be useful alongside planning where to go.

sections.heading: Worrying about toilets is not a diagnosis
sections.html:
The worry may follow a difficult experience, relate to a bowel or bladder condition, come from not knowing the area, or involve several of these things. Looking up toilets before a trip does not by itself mean you have a mental health condition. Physical symptoms should not be dismissed as “just stress” without appropriate assessment.

Fear of situations where escape or help feels difficult can be part of agoraphobia. That does not mean every fear of being unable to find a toilet is agoraphobia. The NHS overview of agoraphobia describes a condition that needs professional assessment. Explaining what happens and how it affects your life is more useful than trying to diagnose yourself.

sections.heading: Make a short, practical plan
sections.html:
Check a toilet near your destination and one alternative. Find out how to enter, when it opens and whether there is a charge. If you are taking a train or coach, check the operator's information about onboard toilets and scheduled stops.

Save the address, charge your phone and allow enough time to get there. You can let someone travelling with you know that you may need a break, without explaining everything that is worrying you.

The purpose of preparation is to help you take part in the activity you planned. If repeated checking takes up a lot of time and you still find it hard to leave home, discuss that pattern with a professional. A toilet map cannot provide complete certainty about every possible situation.

sections.heading: What can help when you feel anxious on the way?
sections.html:
If you need a moment to get your bearings, stop somewhere safe. Identify the next practical step: find the entrance, ask a staff member or walk towards the place you selected. You do not need to solve every possible scenario at once. A companion can help with a specific task, such as reading signs or asking where the toilets are.

Some people find a few minutes of gentle, comfortable breathing helpful when they feel tense. The NHS breathing exercise for stress uses a steady rhythm without forcing the breath. This is a way to settle for a moment, not proof that a physical sensation is caused by anxiety.

Do not use an exercise to ignore a genuine need for a toilet. New, severe or worrying physical symptoms need appropriate medical attention rather than an automatic assumption that anxiety is the cause.

sections.heading: How can a friend or family member help?
sections.html:
Start by acknowledging the difficulty: “I can see that this trip feels stressful.” Ask what would help with the outing, such as company, a slower pace or finding the nearest toilet. A promise that nothing will happen cannot establish whether a particular facility is open.

Avoid teasing, rushing someone or suddenly changing the route to test their confidence. At the same time, allow them to make their own choices. If they are receiving therapy, use the approach to support that they have agreed with their clinician.

A discreet signal for needing a break can be useful when travelling with a group. It lets someone keep their personal situation private.

sections.heading: When is it worth seeking professional support?
sections.html:
Consider seeking help if fear regularly leads you to cancel plans, avoid transport, struggle at work or remain at home. A doctor can assess physical symptoms, while an appropriately qualified mental health professional can help with anxiety. A short note about situations, thoughts and behaviours can make the first conversation easier.

Treatments for some anxiety disorders include cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). The NHS guide to agoraphobia treatment also describes gradual, therapist-guided work. The approach depends on the diagnosis and the individual. This does not mean forcing yourself to disregard physical needs.

You do not need to wait until the problem is severe. You can start with a plain description: “I worry I will not find a toilet, and it is stopping me from going out.”

sections.heading: What can a toilet-finder app do?
sections.html:
Chcę Siku! can help you locate nearby toilets and orient yourself towards a chosen place. It supports the practical task of finding an address and direction. Information may change, and a map cannot promise that every toilet is accessible or open.

The app does not diagnose or treat anxiety. If using it becomes part of distressing, repeated checking, discuss that with your therapist. You can download Chcę Siku! and use our app guide to understand its features. If bowel symptoms are also relevant, read our guide to toilet planning with IBS.

This article is general information. It does not replace an assessment, individual advice or psychological treatment.

title: Finding suitable toilets for older adults when going out
description: Plan walks and journeys with suitable toilets for older adults: check step-free access, opening hours, comfortable routes and individual needs.
author: Chcę Siku! editorial team
lead: A suitable toilet can make a walk, shopping trip or day out easier to plan. For some older adults, a step-free entrance, clear signs and enough time to walk matter as much as distance. Start with the person's own needs and preferences, and support their independence when planning the trip.

sections.heading: Start with the person, not an assumption about age
sections.html:
Not every older person needs more frequent toilet breaks. A useful plan takes account of the person's mobility, health, medication and comfort. If you are planning an outing with a parent, grandparent or friend, ask what would actually help instead of assuming they need assistance with everything.

Bladder leakage becomes more common with age, but it should not be dismissed as something a person must simply accept. NIDDK explains that urinary incontinence is not a routine part of getting older. A healthcare professional can help assess the cause and discuss options. A toilet map supports everyday planning; it does not replace that assessment.

sections.heading: Check whether the toilet is easy to reach
sections.html:
Look beyond the number of metres on the map. Is the entrance at street level? Are there steps, heavy doors or a steep ramp? Is the toilet close to the entrance or at the far end of a long corridor? For someone using a stick, walking frame or wheelchair, these details can matter more than a small difference in distance.

An accessibility symbol does not describe every facility. If grab rails, turning space or room for a companion are important, confirm those details with the venue. Missing information does not prove either that a feature exists or that it is absent.

Check any charge and how to pay. Coins, a card payment or a key obtained from staff are small details that can make a difference on arrival. Our accessible toilet checklist gives more questions to ask.

sections.heading: Build a comfortable break into the journey
sections.html:
Choose a toilet near your destination and check its opening hours. A park can remain open after its toilets close; a station's toilet may have different access rules from its main hall. On a longer journey, check the interchange or planned rest stop too.

Allow for the person's walking pace. A time estimate on a phone is only a guide. Look for suitable crossings, somewhere to rest and enough time to avoid rushing. The route matters as much as the facilities inside the building.

A simple backup can be useful: another nearby venue or a phone number for staff. Write the details on paper if that is easier to use while travelling. Agree on breaks together rather than making the person's decisions for them.

sections.heading: Do not deliberately become dehydrated to avoid toilets
sections.html:
Drinking too little can lead to dehydration. If bladder symptoms make fluid planning difficult, ask a healthcare professional about amounts and timing, especially if other conditions or prescribed fluid restrictions apply. NIDDK recommends individual advice about fluids, rather than restricting them to the point of dehydration.

Do not change the timing or dose of prescribed medicines on your own before a journey. If a medicine makes outings difficult to plan, discuss this with a doctor or pharmacist. Pack the supplies you normally need and follow the advice already given for your situation.

A calm, practical approach helps when travelling together: “There is a toilet on the way; we can stop there.” There is no need to comment on how often someone uses the bathroom or compare them with other people.

sections.heading: When should bladder symptoms be assessed?
sections.html:
Discuss recurring urgency, urine leakage, difficulty passing urine or frequent night-time toilet visits with a healthcare professional. Also mention if worry about toilet access is making you give up walks or social activities. It may help to bring a note of when the problem began, how it has changed and which medicines you take.

Being unable to pass urine or empty the bladder, blood in the urine, and painful urination need prompt medical attention. These warning signs are covered in the NIDDK guide to bladder-control symptoms. New symptoms should not be explained away solely by age.

sections.heading: Use a phone as a practical aid
sections.html:
Chcę Siku! lets you look up nearby toilets, read available details and see the direction to a selected place. If someone is new to the app, try the steps together at home, then on a short familiar outing. Allow time for the person to make their own choices.

After a visit, a review about the entrance or cleanliness can help others. Confirm essential facilities with the venue when the listing does not provide enough detail, because information can change. Download Chcę Siku! and see how to find and review a toilet.

This article provides general information. It does not replace individual medical advice or an assessment of a particular venue's accessibility.

NIDDK - Symptoms & Causes of Bladder Control Problems
NIDDK - Treatments for Bladder Control Problems

title: How to find an accessible toilet that meets your needs
description: An accessible toilet is more than a wheelchair symbol. Check the route, entrance, transfer space, equipment and access rules before setting off.
author: Chcę Siku! editorial team
lead: To find a suitable accessible toilet, start with the accessibility filter, then check the route, entrance and equipment against your own needs. A wheelchair symbol is a useful starting point, but it cannot explain the steps on the way, space to manoeuvre or whether there is room for an assistant.

sections.heading: Accessibility depends on the person using the toilet
sections.html:
A wheelchair user, someone using crutches and someone with a walking frame may need different facilities. The way a person transfers, assistance they need and whether they can open a door independently also matter. Start with a short list of the conditions that are essential for you.

The U.S. Access Board guide to toilet rooms considers doors, manoeuvring space, fixtures and equipment. These are useful areas to ask about when checking a venue. The guide explains US requirements; it should not be treated as the law in every country.

sections.heading: Use the accessibility filter in Chcę Siku!
sections.html:
Open the app, allow it to use your location and select “Dla osób z niepełnosprawnościami” (for people with disabilities). You can add other requirements, such as a free toilet. The list looks for places marked with all the selected features and orders nearby results by distance. We show the Polish button wording here so you can recognise it in the app.

Read the description, look at photos and check comments. A label in a community map is not an accessibility certificate or confirmation of every measurement. If an important detail is missing, ask the venue directly. An unmarked place is not necessarily inaccessible either; its information may be incomplete.

sections.heading: Check the whole route from the street to the door
sections.html:
A well-equipped toilet can still be difficult to reach if there are steps at the building entrance. Ask where the step-free route starts and whether it is open at the time of your visit. If it involves a lift, check its location and whether it is working. Find out whether an alternative entrance requires help from a member of staff.

In the app, “Prowadź” (guide me) shows a map and direction towards the destination. It does not guarantee a step-free route. A standard walking route in another map app also cannot confirm all the conditions you need. Check the crossings and entrance to the building separately.

sections.heading: Questions to ask about the toilet itself
sections.html:
• Will the doorway and passage fit the mobility equipment I use?
  • Is there space to turn and approach the toilet from the side I need?
  • Can I reach the grab rails, basin and other equipment from my position?
  • Is there enough room for someone assisting me?
  • Is a key or code required, and where can I obtain it?
  • When is the toilet accessible, and does it close with the rest of the building?

A specific dimension or need is easier to answer than a general question about whether the toilet is “adapted”. On arrival, check whether temporary objects or stored equipment obstruct the space.

sections.heading: Accessible toilets and Changing Places facilities are different
sections.html:
Some people also need a hoist, an adult-sized changing bench and space for assistants. Changing Places explains the additional equipment and space its facilities provide, beyond a standard accessible toilet. Its official information can help you identify this type of facility.

Do not assume that the app's “Przewijak” (baby-changing table) filter means there is an adult changing bench. Likewise, the accessibility filter does not confirm Changing Places equipment. If you need a particular device, contact the venue to confirm its presence and whether it is available for use. This is especially useful when planning a journey abroad.

sections.heading: Share details that help the next visitor
sections.html:
After visiting, describe what you actually checked: an entrance from the courtyard, a key held by security, the lift's location or an obstruction you found. Rather than deciding whether the toilet suits everyone, give others the facts they can compare with their own needs. Include the date of your visit when helpful.

A photograph of an empty entrance or the facilities can add useful information if it respects other people's privacy. Our Chcę Siku! guide explains how to add details after signing in. Download the app to look up nearby places, and see our travel guide for planning toilet stops in unfamiliar areas.
